blocks.text: Aaj hum ek bohat practical sawal se shuru karte hain: kisi function ka graph kahan upar ja raha hai aur kahan neeche aa raha hai? Sochiye aap ek pahari raaste par chal rahe hain. Kabhi charhai aati hai (upar ja rahe hain), kabhi utraai (neeche aa rahe hain). Function ke graph par left se right chalna bilkul aisa hi hai. Charhai wale hisse ko increasing aur utraai wale hisse ko decreasing kehte hain. Is sabaq mein hum yeh seekhenge ke derivative ki madad se yeh kaise pata karte hain, bina graph banaye.

rows: Maan lijiye \(I\) ek interval hai aur \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) ek function hai. Hum kehte hain ke \(f\) increasing hai agar \(I\) ke kisi bhi do numbers \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) ke liye \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \le f(x_{2})\).

Maan lijiye \(I\) ek interval hai aur \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) ek function hai. Hum kehte hain ke \(f\) decreasing hai agar \(I\) ke kisi bhi do numbers \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) ke liye \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \ge f(x_{2})\).
blocks.caption: Increasing aur decreasing functions (kitab ki definitions)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Aasaan alfaaz mein: \(f\) increasing hai jab bara input kabhi chhota output na de, yani graph left se right chalte hue kabhi neeche na aaye. Decreasing tab hai jab graph kabhi upar na jaye.
Kitab ne \(\le\) aur \(\ge\) use kiya hai, is liye beech mein seedha (flat) hissa bhi chal jata hai. Agar humein bilkul upar hi upar jana chahiye to \(f(x_{1}) < f(x_{2})\) likhte hain (strictly increasing), aur bilkul neeche hi neeche ke liye \(f(x_{1}) > f(x_{2})\) (strictly decreasing).
Yeh lafz hamesha kisi interval ke saath bole jate hain. Misaal: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) interval \((-\infty, 0]\) par decreasing hai aur \([0, \infty)\) par increasing, lekin poori real line par na increasing hai na decreasing.

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text: \((a, b)\), \([a, b]\), \((a, b]\), \([a, b)\), \((-\infty, a)\), \((-\infty, \infty)\), \((-\infty, a]\), \((a, \infty)\), \([a, \infty)\) all are intervals.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Interval (number line ka ek lagataar, bina toote hissa) yaad kar lijiye. Gol bracket ( ) ka matlab hai end point shamil nahin, square bracket [ ] ka matlab hai end point shamil hai. \(\infty\) koi number nahin, sirf "bina had ke" ka ishara hai, is liye us ke saath hamesha gol bracket aata hai.
Ab asal kaam ki baat. Maan lijiye \(f\) ek differentiable function hai jo interval \(I\) par defined hai. To

items: (i) \(f\) interval \(I\) par increasing hai, agar har \(x \in I\) ke liye \(f'(x) \ge 0\).
(ii) \(f\) interval \(I\) par decreasing hai, agar har \(x \in I\) ke liye \(f'(x) \le 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Derivative ka sign hi kyun faisla karta hai? Yaad kijiye, \(f'(x)\) us point par tangent line (graph ko chhoo kar guzarne wali line) ka slope hai (2.7).
Slope positive ho to tangent, aur us ke saath graph, right ki taraf upar uthta hai. Slope negative ho to right ki taraf neeche girta hai. Bilkul jaise pahari raaste par paon ke neeche zameen ka jhukaao batata hai ke aap charh rahe hain ya utar rahe hain.
Is liye har do points ki values compare karne ke bajaye (jo lakhon jore hain, ek ek kar ke mumkin hi nahin), hum sirf ek cheez check karte hain: interval par \(f'(x)\) ka sign.

blocks.title: Khud sochiye
blocks.text: \(f(x) = 5x + 3\) ke liye \(f'(x) = 5\). Yeh function kahan increasing hai? Aur \(g(x) = -3x\) kahan decreasing hai? (Jawab: \(f'(x) = 5 > 0\) har jagah, is liye \(f\) poori real line par increasing; \(g'(x) = -3 < 0\), is liye \(g\) poori real line par decreasing. Seedhi line ka slope hi us ka derivative hai.)

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Prove that \(f(x) = e^{x}\) defined on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\) is increasing.
steps:
Diya gaya: \(f(x) = e^{x}\), poori real line \((-\infty, \infty)\) par.
Maloom karna (prove karna): \(f\) increasing hai.
Tareeqa: \(f\) differentiable hai, is liye test (i) lagayenge: agar interval ke har \(x\) par \(f'(x) \ge 0\) ho to \(f\) increasing hai. Yani humein sirf \(f'(x)\) ka sign dekhna hai; har do numbers ko compare karne ki zaroorat nahin.

Step 1: Derivative nikaalein
\[f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x}\right) = e^{x}\]
Kyun: \(e^{x}\) woh khaas function hai jiska derivative woh khud hai (2.5 mein parha tha). Is liye yahan koi extra factor nahin aata.

Step 2: \(f'(x)\) ka sign dekhein
\[f'(x) = e^{x} > 0\]
\[\text{for each } x \in (-\infty, \infty)\]
Kyun: \(e \approx 2.718\) ek positive number hai, aur positive number ki koi bhi power (chahe negative ho, jaise \(e^{-5}\)) positive hi rehti hai. \(e^{-5}\) bohat chhota hai magar zero ya negative nahin. Is liye \(e^{x}\) kabhi zero ya negative nahin hota.

Step 3: Natija likhein
Poori real line par \(f'(x) > 0\) hai, is liye \(f(x) = e^{x}\) interval \((-\infty, \infty)\) par increasing hai.
Kyun: yeh test (i) hai. \(> 0\) to \(\ge 0\) se bhi mazboot shart hai, is liye test poora ho gaya.

Tasdeeq: do numbers lein, \(x_{1} = 0 < x_{2} = 1\).
\[f(0) = 1 < f(1) = e \approx 2.718\]
Bara input, bara output: bilkul wahi jo definition kehti hai. Graph left se right ki taraf hamesha upar ja raha hai.
blocks.answer: \(f'(x) = e^{x} > 0\) har real \(x\) ke liye, is liye \(f(x) = e^{x}\) interval \((-\infty, \infty)\) par increasing hai.

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: Show that \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) defined on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\) is decreasing.
steps:
Diya gaya: \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\), poori real line par.
Maloom karna (show karna): \(f\) decreasing hai.
Tareeqa: test (ii): agar har \(x\) par \(f'(x) \le 0\) ho to \(f\) decreasing hai. Derivative ke liye \(a^{u}\) wala rule aur chain rule lagayenge, kyun ke yahan base 2 hai aur power \(-x\) hai.

Step 1: Sahi derivative
\[f'(x) = 2^{-x}\ln 2 \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(-x)\]
\[= 2^{-x}\ln 2 \cdot (-1)\]
\[f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2\]
Kyun: rule hai \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(a^{u}\right) = a^{u}\ln a \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\). Yahan \(a = 2\) aur \(u = -x\), to \(\frac{du}{dx} = -1\).
Dhyan dein: kitab yahan \(\ln 2\) ka factor likhna bhool gayi hai (neeche "Kitab ki ghalti" dekhiye). \(\ln\) wala factor sirf base \(e\) ke liye ghayab hota hai, kyun ke \(\ln e = 1\). Base 2 ke liye \(\ln 2\) zaroor aata hai.

Step 2: \(f'(x)\) ka sign
\[2^{-x} > 0,\quad \ln 2 \approx 0.693 > 0\]
\[f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\]
Kyun: \(2^{-x}\) positive hai (positive base ki har power positive), \(\ln 2\) bhi positive hai kyun ke \(2 > 1\). Do positive cheezon ka product positive, aur aage minus ka nishaan use negative bana deta hai.

Step 3: Natija
Har \(x\) par \(f'(x) < 0\), is liye \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) poori real line par decreasing hai.
Kyun: test (ii). Ghor karein: \(\ln 2\) ki ghalti se jawab nahin badla, kyun ke \(\ln 2\) positive hai aur sign wohi rehta hai. Lekin exam mein sahi derivative likhna zaroori hai, warna marks katenge.

Tasdeeq: \(x_{1} = 0 < x_{2} = 1\) lein.
\[f(0) = 2^{0} = 1 > f(1) = 2^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\]
Bara input, chhota output: graph neeche ja raha hai. Asal mein \(2^{-x} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\), aur 1 se chhote base wala exponential hamesha decreasing hota hai (Unit 1).
blocks.answer: \(f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\) har real \(x\) ke liye, is liye \(f(x) = 2^{-x}\) interval \((-\infty, \infty)\) par decreasing hai.

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text: Example 16 mein kitab \(f'(x) = 2^{-x}\frac{d}{dx}(-x)\) aur phir \(f'(x) = -2^{-x} < 0\) likhti hai. \(a^{u}\) ka derivative \(a^{u}\ln a\,\frac{du}{dx}\) hota hai, is liye \(\ln 2\) ka factor reh gaya hai. Sahi: \(f'(x) = -2^{-x}\ln 2 < 0\). \(\ln 2 > 0\) hai, is liye sign aur natija (decreasing) wohi rehte hain.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: Kitab "Example 16" ka number do dafa chhaapti hai: yahan (\(f(x) = 2^{-x}\)) aur phir 2.9.1 mein (\(f(x) = |x|\)). Hum dono printed numbers waise hi rakhte hain taa ke aap kitab ke label se har example dhoond sakein.

blocks.title: Hamari taraf se misaal
blocks.text:
\(f(x) = x^{3} + x\) lijiye. \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} + 1\).
\(x^{2}\) kabhi negative nahin hota, is liye \(3x^{2} \ge 0\) aur \(3x^{2} + 1 \ge 1 > 0\).
Yani har jagah \(f'(x) > 0\): \(f(x) = x^{3} + x\) poori real line par increasing hai. Dekha? Graph banaye baghair sirf derivative ke sign se jawab mil gaya.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: "Prove that \(f\) is increasing" wale sawal mein teen lines zaroor likhiye: (1) derivative, (2) us ka sign wajah ke saath (jaise "kyun ke \(e^{x} > 0\) har \(x\) ke liye"), (3) natija interval ke naam ke saath. Examiner yahi teen cheezein dhoondta hai.

blocks.title: Yaad rakhne wali baatein
blocks.text:
1. Increasing: \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \le f(x_{2})\); decreasing: \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow f(x_{1}) \ge f(x_{2})\).
2. Differentiable \(f\) ke liye: interval par \(f'(x) \ge 0\) to increasing, \(f'(x) \le 0\) to decreasing.
3. Hamesha interval ka naam lijiye; ek hi function kisi interval par barhta aur kisi par ghatta ho sakta hai.
4. \(e^{x}\) poori real line par increasing hai; \(2^{-x} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\) poori real line par decreasing hai.

blocks.title: Aam ghaltiyan
blocks.text:
1. \(a^{x}\) ke derivative mein \(\ln a\) bhool jana: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{-x}\right) = -2^{-x}\ln 2\) hai, sirf \(-2^{-x}\) nahin.
2. "\(f\) increasing hai" likh dena aur interval na batana.
3. \(f'(x)\) ke bajaye \(f(x)\) ka sign dekh lena: \(2^{-x}\) hamesha positive hai, phir bhi decreasing hai. Barhna ya ghatna derivative batata hai, function ki apni value nahin.
